plan.title: What people clock in ten seconds
Your red flag (yes, you have one)
What you have too much of, and what you dodge
Okay fine, the fix (Bom made me)

strong.text:
Yeon's add-on for strong charts: whatever first impression you make, it lands harder than you think. You walk in with a fully formed opinion of the room, and the room can feel it. Some people find that magnetic. Others decide in ten seconds that you're a lot, and they never tell you, they just sit at the other end of the table.

Try one experiment at your next new-people event. Ask three questions before you share one opinion. Not interview questions, curious ones. What are you into lately? How do you know the host? You'll still make your impression. It'll just include the information that you're interested in other people, which is the part strong charts accidentally leave out. Same you, better reviews.

Also, check your face. Strong charts often have a resting expression that says "I've already decided about you." You haven't, usually. You're just thinking. But people read faces before they hear a word. Relax your jaw, look at whoever is talking, nod once in a while. Tiny adjustments, huge difference in how many people come over to talk to you.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Three questions before one opinion. Try it once. Watch the room relax.

weak.text:
Yeon's add-on for weak charts: you make the impression above and then undercut it. A nervous joke, an apology for talking, a quick retreat into the polite, agreeable version of you. People assume that's the whole show. Months later they discover how funny and opinionated you really are, and they feel a bit cheated, like they got the trailer for a different film.

Try leading with one real thing. A strong opinion about something low-stakes, pineapple on pizza, the best season, which friend in the group would survive a horror movie. Small, specific, yours. Weak charts hold back the good stuff until they feel safe. Let a little out early. The right people will find you faster, and the wrong ones were never going to get the director's cut anyway.

And stop apologizing for taking up the first thirty seconds. Weak charts introduce themselves like they're interrupting: "Hi, sorry, I'm, um, a friend of Sam's." Try "Hi, I'm" and your name, said like it's good news. It is good news. You're about to be one of the more interesting people they meet tonight.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Lead with one real opinion. Pizza counts. Stop handing out the trailer version.

strong.text:
Strong-chart footnote: your red flag comes with a defense attorney. When someone points it out, you explain why it's actually reasonable, with examples, possibly with a slide deck. Very convincing. Also the reason nobody points it out twice.

Here's the test. The next time someone names your flag, say only "Huh. Tell me more." Then stop. No rebuttal, no context, no "to be fair." Let the feedback sit in the room for a full minute. You don't have to agree. You just have to stop winning the conversation long enough to hear it. People who can take a hit without swinging back are rare, and everyone trusts them a little more.

One more thing. Strong charts tend to believe their flag is a strength that other people are too sensitive to handle. Sometimes that's true. Mostly, it's a convenient story. If three different people in different parts of your life have mentioned the same thing, that isn't sensitivity. That's a pattern, and patterns are worth an honest look.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: No rebuttal. No slide deck. Just listen for one full minute.

weak.text:
Weak-chart footnote: your red flag hides behind an apology. You say sorry before anyone's annoyed, you check if things are okay three times, you explain yourself before anyone asked. It looks like being considerate. It actually puts other people in the job of reassuring you, constantly, which is its own kind of demanding.

Here's the test. For one week, count your unnecessary sorries. Every "sorry to bother you," every "sorry, quick question," every "sorry if that's weird." Then replace half of them with "thanks." Thanks for waiting. Thanks for listening. Same politeness, completely different energy. You stop asking for forgiveness and start offering appreciation, which people enjoy receiving a lot more.

And notice the flag underneath the apology: resentment. When you've over-apologized and over-accommodated for a while, it all comes back as a cold silence or a sudden sharp sentence that shocks everyone. Saying what you want early is how you stop that from happening. Clear and early beats nice and then furious.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Count your sorries this week. Swap half for thanks. Different energy entirely.

strong.text:
Strong charts sabotage love by running it. You know how the relationship should go, so you steer, and for a while your partner enjoys being driven somewhere nice. Then they notice they haven't picked the destination in eight months, and they get quiet, and you can't work out why, because everything is going so well.

Hand over the wheel once a month. Let them plan the weekend, pick the holiday, decide something that matters. Then do the hard part: enjoy it, or at least don't critique it in the car home. A partner who never gets to lead eventually stops showing up as a full person. And you deserve a full person, not a very loyal passenger.

And watch for the scorekeeping. Strong charts often run a ledger: who planned, who paid, who apologized. Nobody agreed to the ledger, but you're keeping it anyway, and when it tips the wrong way, you go cold. Burn the ledger. Love isn't a fair trade, it's two people taking turns being generous, sometimes unevenly, for a long time.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Let them pick the holiday. And no critique on the drive home.

weak.text:
Weak charts sabotage love by disappearing into it. You adapt to their schedule, their friends, their music, their opinions about your friends. It feels like closeness. It slowly turns you into a supporting character in your own relationship, and partners don't fall deeper for supporting characters. They get bored, and they can't explain why.

Keep three things that are only yours. A hobby, a friend group, a Saturday morning routine, whatever. Defend them politely and consistently. Not because you need space from your partner, but because a relationship needs two whole people in it. The version of you with your own stuff going on is the one they fell for in the first place.

Also, notice if you pick partners who need fixing. Weak charts often feel safest with someone who needs them, because being needed feels like a guarantee. It isn't. It's a job. Look for someone who wants you, not someone who requires you. The difference is enormous and it shows up in about three months.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Your hobby, your friends, your Saturday. Not negotiable. Politely.

strong.text:
Strong-chart receipt: at work, you're the one who gets it done, and the one who redoes other people's parts because yours is the right way. Efficient? Sure. It also teaches everyone around you that their work will be overwritten anyway, so why try. Then you complain about doing everything. Yeon has seen this film.

With friends, you're loyal and you have opinions about their life choices. Free advice, generously given, rarely requested. This week, try one rule: before advising anyone, ask "Do you want my take, or do you want to vent?" Respect the answer. You'll keep your influence, and your friends will start bringing you the important stuff instead of only the easy stuff.

One more receipt: you're great in a crisis and terrible at the boring middle. You'll save the project at the last minute and then lose interest in the follow-up. Your coworkers love the rescue and quietly dread the next phase. Stay for one boring follow-up meeting this month. Being reliable in the dull parts is what turns respect into trust.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Ask 'Do you want my take?' before giving it. Revolutionary, I know.

weak.text:
Weak-chart receipt: in the office, you're the dependable yes-person who then stays late doing the yes. You're liked, you're useful, and you're slightly invisible at promotion time, because you never mentioned what you did. People assume quiet work happened by itself.

With friends, you're the listener and the helper, and you rarely ask for anything back. Then one day you're sad and realize nobody knows how to look after you, because you never let them practice. Two moves for this month. At work, send one short message about something you finished and how it went. With friends, ask one person for one small favor. Both will feel awkward. Both will work.

One more receipt: you're everyone's emergency contact and nobody's first call for fun. People think of you when they need help, not when they're planning the good stuff. Change that by inviting them first. Plan the dinner, start the trip idea, suggest the movie. Being the fun friend is a role you can choose, not one you have to be assigned.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Tell your boss what you finished. Ask a friend for one favor. Awkward, effective.

strong.text:
Bonus lie for strong charts: "I'm just being honest." Sometimes you are. Sometimes honesty is the costume your impatience wears to the party. The tell is timing. Honesty that arrives when someone can do something with it is a gift. Honesty that arrives when you're irritated, in front of other people, mostly serves you.

Before the next blunt truth, ask yourself two quick questions. Is this useful to them right now? Would I say it the same way if they were my boss? If the answers are no and no, hold it for a better moment. You lose nothing. The truth keeps. And when you do say it, it lands as care instead of a hit.

There's a second lie hiding behind the first one: "I don't need anyone." Strong charts say it with a straight face. It's not true. You need people who'll tell you the truth, people who'll celebrate you, people who'll sit with you when the strong act runs out. Needing them doesn't make you smaller. It makes you human, which is allowed even for you.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Honest and irritated is just irritated. Wait an hour, then be honest.

weak.text:
Bonus lie for weak charts: "I don't mind." You mind. You mind about the restaurant, the plan, the way they spoke to you on Tuesday. You say you don't because minding feels like a burden you'd be placing on someone. But the minding doesn't vanish, it just files itself away and comes back as tiredness, or a sudden sharp comment three weeks later.

Practice minding small things out loud. "Actually, I'd prefer the other place." "That joke stung a bit." Low stakes, plain voice, no apology. Every time you do it and nothing explodes, the lie gets weaker. People who love you would rather know. People who don't were going to leave anyway.

There's a second lie hiding behind the first one: "They'd be better off without me bothering them." Weak charts tell themselves this right before going quiet. It's almost never true. Most people are glad to hear from you. The ones who aren't will make it clear, and then you can stop texting them with a clean conscience.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: You do mind. Say 'I'd prefer the other place.' Watch nothing explode.

strong.text:
Bom's extra for strong charts, delivered under protest by Yeon: your fix needs one soft habit. Pick something you'd normally find a bit pointless. Asking how someone's weekend was and listening to the whole answer. Sending a thank-you message for a small thing. Admitting you were wrong about something minor, out loud, in front of a witness.

Do it every day for two weeks. Strong charts change through practice, not through insight, because you already know the insight and you've already argued with it. The soft habit won't make you weaker. It'll make your strength easier to be around, which means more people will let you lead. Yeon calls this a win. Bom calls it growth. Same thing.

And a maintenance tip: check in with one person a month and ask how you've been to deal with lately. Not fishing for compliments, actually asking. Strong charts drift back into old habits when nobody's reflecting them. Someone with permission to say "you've been a bit much lately" is worth more than any reading, including this one.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: One soft habit a day for two weeks. Yeon says it's a win. It is.

weak.text:
Bom's extra for weak charts, which Yeon approved: your fix needs one brave habit. Something small that requires taking up space. Speak first in one meeting a week. Choose the restaurant every time someone asks. Send the message you've been drafting for days without rereading it.

Do it every day for two weeks, even badly. Weak charts change through evidence. You need to see, again and again, that taking up a little space doesn't cost you the people you love. It usually does the opposite. They relax, because they finally know what you want. By the end of the two weeks, you won't be a different person. You'll just be easier to find.

And a maintenance tip: keep a tiny list of times you took up space and it went fine. The meeting where you spoke first. The time you said no and the friendship survived. Weak charts forget the evidence and remember the fear. Reread the list on wobbly days. It's proof you're allowed to be here, in full.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: One brave little habit a day. You'll be easier to find. In the best way.

peer_strong.text:
Your chart is heavy on {dm_el}, your own element. Saju calls that the peer family: siblings, rivals, people who look like you. Yeon's translation: you're surrounded by yourself. That makes you self-reliant, stubborn and competitive about things nobody else realized were a competition. Who's busier. Who's more tired. Who had the worse commute. You don't ask for help because you'd rather struggle than owe, and you secretly keep score of who helped whom.

The brutal part: people stop offering. Not because they don't care, but because you made it clear you'd rather do it yourself. Accept the next offer of help, even if you could do it faster. It's not about the task. It's about letting someone in. Bonus truth: you're the friend who gives the best advice and takes none. Try taking one piece this month.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Your chart is basically a mirror. Stop competing with your friends about who's tired.

output_strong.text:
Your chart is heavy on {heavy_el}, the element your {dm_el} produces. That's the output family: talent, wit, expression, opinions. With a strong chart behind it, you're the funniest person in the group chat and the one most likely to say the thing everyone regrets laughing at. Output also hates rules, so you test authority for sport, whether it's your boss, your landlord or a sign that says please don't.

Yeon's verdict: the talent is real and the filter is optional. Pick one setting where you keep the sharp line to yourself, work meetings or family dinners. Not forever, just enough to notice how much smoother life gets when not every thought gets published. Bonus truth: you're charming enough to get away with a lot. That's exactly why it's worth not testing it every day.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Heavy {heavy_el}. Funny, sharp, and allergic to rules. Pick one place to keep the filter on.

wealth_strong.text:
Your chart is heavy on {heavy_el}, the element your {dm_el} controls. That's the wealth family: what you go after and manage. On a strong chart you're the operator. Plans, budgets, logistics, a spreadsheet for the friend trip. You get things done and you like being in control of outcomes, including other people's.

The brutal part: people feel managed around you, even when you're being helpful. Your partner doesn't want a project manager. Your friends don't want a performance review of their dating life. Let one thing in your week be run badly by somebody else and don't fix it. The world will survive. So will you, eventually. Bonus truth: some of your control is anxiety in a blazer. If letting go feels impossible, ask what you're afraid will happen.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Heavy {heavy_el}: you run everything. Let one thing be run badly this week.

power_strong.text:
Your chart is heavy on {heavy_el}, the element that controls your {dm_el}. That's the power family: rules, duty, status, the inner boss. A strong chart wears it well. You're disciplined, responsible, and you care what's right. You also judge, quietly and constantly, yourself first, everyone else a close second.

Yeon's verdict: your standards are high and your patience is low. When people don't meet the bar, you go cool and correct. That makes you trustworthy and slightly exhausting to work with. Try saying one appreciation for every correction. It costs nothing and it means people will keep bringing you their work instead of hiding it. Bonus truth: the person you judge hardest is you. Lower the bar for yourself first. Everyone else gets the benefit.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Heavy {heavy_el}: an inner judge with no off switch. One praise per correction.

resource_strong.text:
Your chart is heavy on {heavy_el}, the element that feeds your {dm_el}. That's the resource family: learning, comfort, protection. You're well read, self-sufficient and very good at thinking. Also very good at thinking instead of doing. You've researched the gym, the course and the move for months, and you've done none of them.

The brutal part: comfort is your favorite hiding place. Your couch has seen more of your ambition than anyone else. Pick one thing you've been researching and start it badly this week. Not perfectly, not after one more article. Badly, today. Resource energy turns into wisdom only when it gets used. Bonus truth: you'd make an excellent teacher if you ever finished the course. Finish the course.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Heavy {heavy_el}: you've researched everything and started nothing. Start badly.

output_weak.text:
Your chart leans on {heavy_el}, the element your {dm_el} produces. That's the output family: giving, entertaining, performing. On a weak chart it drains you. You're the entertainer of the group, the one who keeps things fun, and you go home exhausted and slightly empty.

Yeon's verdict: you're performing likability. You don't have to. People who only like you when you're on are not your people. Go to the next gathering and be quiet for the first hour. Let someone else carry the conversation. The ones who still seek you out are the ones worth keeping, and you'll have energy left for yourself. Bonus truth: the people who only want the fun version of you are not friends. They're an audience. Know the difference.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Leaning {heavy_el}: you perform likability and go home empty. Be quiet for an hour.

wealth_weak.text:
Your chart leans on {heavy_el}, the element your {dm_el} controls. That's the wealth family: what you try to hold and manage. Classical readers call this wealth heavy, self light: too much to carry with too little behind you. You take on responsibilities you can't sustain, other people's problems, other people's moods, other people's deadlines.

Yeon's verdict: you're not a support beam. Every time you say yes to carrying something for someone else, ask yourself what you're putting down to make room. Usually it's your sleep or your own plans. Put down one thing this week that was never yours to hold. Bonus truth: you can't make everyone okay. It was never your job, and you're doing it on an empty tank.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Leaning {heavy_el}: you carry everyone's stuff. Put one bag down. Not yours anyway.

power_weak.text:
Your chart leans on {heavy_el}, the element that controls your {dm_el}. That's the power family: pressure, rules, judgment. On a weak chart it shows up as a constant feeling of being evaluated. You check your tone, reread your emails, replay conversations to see if you said something wrong. Spoiler: you usually didn't.

Yeon's verdict: the critic in your head is wrong more often than right. It's just loud. Next time it starts, ask it for evidence. Not feelings, evidence. Most of the time it has none. Then go and do the thing anyway, with the critic grumbling in the back seat. Bonus truth: nobody is grading you as harshly as you're grading yourself. Most people are too busy worrying about their own grades.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Leaning {heavy_el}: your inner critic has zero evidence. Make it show receipts.

rooted_on_paper.text: Yeon's version: you look tougher than you feel. People assume you're fine because the chart looks full, and you play along because admitting a wobble feels embarrassing. Then you crash privately. Stop doing the tough act for people who'd happily help. Tell one person when you're not okay, before it's a crisis. Bonus truth: needing support doesn't mean you're fake strong. It means you're strong in the normal, human way.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: You look tough, you feel wobbly. Tell one person before it's a crisis.

output_strong.text: {miss_el} is missing from your visible chart. For your {dm_el}, that's the output element: expression. Yeon's translation: you feel everything and say almost nothing, until you say all of it at once. People think you're calm, and then you erupt over a dishwasher. Let feelings out in smaller portions. A short "that annoyed me" on the day beats a monologue in a month. Smaller vents, more often. Your furniture will thank you.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: No {miss_el}: calm for weeks, then a full eruption about the dishwasher. Vent smaller.

wealth_strong.text: {miss_el} is missing from your visible chart. For your {dm_el}, that's the wealth element: pursuit and follow-through. You have energy and ideas and a suspicious lack of finished projects. Strong charts without wealth start things. Pick one, finish it, and show someone the finished thing. Yes, even the boring last ten percent. Finished beats brilliant. Every time.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: No {miss_el}: twelve projects at ninety percent. Finish one. Show it to someone.

power_strong.text: {miss_el} is missing from your visible chart. For your {dm_el}, that's the power element: rules and limits. You make your own rules, change them when convenient, and are honestly surprised when people expect you to be on time. Borrow some structure from outside. A calendar you actually use. A friend who can say "you said you'd do this." Being on time is a love language. Learn it.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: No {miss_el}: your rules change whenever it suits you. Use a calendar. A real one.

resource_strong.text: {miss_el} is missing from your visible chart. For your {dm_el}, that's the resource element: rest and being looked after. You're strong and you run on fumes and pride. You'd rather pull an all-nighter than ask for help. Yeon's verdict: that's not toughness, that's bad planning with good branding. Sleep. Accept help. Let someone bring you food. Rest isn't weakness. It's maintenance.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: No {miss_el}: running on fumes and calling it character.

output_weak.text: {miss_el} is missing from your visible chart. For your {dm_el}, that's the output element: expression. On a weak chart it keeps you from overspending your energy, which is smart. It also means nobody knows what you think. In meetings, in friendships, in love. Say one opinion a day out loud. Even a tiny one. Your opinion is allowed in the room.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: No {miss_el}: your opinions are a state secret. Declassify one.

wealth_weak.text: {miss_el} is missing from your visible chart. For your {dm_el}, that's the wealth element: going after things. You wait to be offered: the job, the date, the invitation. Sometimes it comes. Often someone louder gets it first. Ask for one thing this week that you'd normally wait to be offered. Asking is not the same as being pushy.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: No {miss_el}: you wait politely while louder people get served.

power_weak.text: {miss_el} is missing from your visible chart. For your {dm_el}, that's the power element: outside pressure. Good news, fewer bosses in your head. Bad news, you might drift without deadlines. Set one gentle deadline for something you care about and tell someone. Not to pressure you, to remind you it matters. Deadlines can be kind. Pick a gentle one.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: No {miss_el}: nobody's chasing you. So you drift. Set one deadline. Tell a friend.

resource_weak.text: {miss_el} is missing from your visible chart. For your {dm_el}, that's the resource element: the support that feeds you. Which explains why you're so hungry for approval. Not a flaw, a gap. Fill it on purpose: people who are kind to you, rest, learning something just for you. Then approval stops being a survival need and goes back to being a nice extra. You deserve kindness without having to earn it first.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: No {miss_el}: that's why approval feels like oxygen. Get your oxygen elsewhere.

none_strong.text: All five elements show up in your pillars, even if some hide in the branches. Yeon's translation: you have a tool for everything and you mostly use the hammer. You could be diplomatic, patient or playful. You choose blunt because it's fastest. Try a different tool once a day and notice it works better than you'd assume. Different tools, same you, better results.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Five elements, and you use the hammer every time. Diplomacy exists.

none_weak.text: All five elements show up in your pillars, even if some hide in the branches. Yeon's translation: you're more capable than you act. You have the tools to be firm, funny and clear. You just keep picking the safest one, polite. Pick the brave one once this week. Spoiler: it'll go fine. Brave once a week is a great start.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: You have all five tools. You keep using 'polite.' Pick the brave one once.

resource.title: Your fix element: {helper_el}
resource.text: Every chart has an element that rebalances it. For your weak {dm_el} chart, it's {helper_el}, the one that nourishes your Day Master. Yeon's translation: you don't need more pressure or more effort. You need refueling. Most of the flaws in this reading get smaller when you're well fed in {helper_el} terms, because a fed chart doesn't have to people-please, overwork or hide. Less grit, more fuel. That's the actual fix. Yeon's practical version: before you try to fix any flaw in this reading, check whether you're running on empty. Half of them disappear after a good week of sleep and kindness.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Your fix element is {helper_el}. Less grit, more fuel. Seriously.

peer.title: Your fix element: {helper_el}, your own element
peer.text: Every chart has an element that rebalances it. Yours already holds plenty of nourishment on paper, so the fix is your own element, {helper_el}. Translation: stop collecting advice and start collecting allies. People at your level who'll tell you the truth and stand next to you while you act on it. You don't need another podcast. You need a friend with a spine. Yeon's practical version: find one friend who'll be honest with you and one who'll cheer for you. Ideally the same person. Keep them.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Your fix element is {helper_el}. Stop collecting advice. Collect allies.

output.title: Your fix element: {helper_el}
output.text: Every chart has an element that rebalances it. A strong {dm_el} chart needs an outlet, and yours is {helper_el}, the element your Day Master produces. Translation: your flaws get worse when you sit on your energy. Bossiness, stubbornness and judging are what strength does when it's bored. Give it work: make something, teach something, move your body, put the force somewhere useful. Yeon's practical version: when you catch yourself being bossy, ask what you're not doing with your own energy. Then go do that instead.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Your fix element is {helper_el}. Bored strength turns bossy. Give it a job.

wealth.title: Your fix element: {helper_el}
wealth.text: Every chart has an element that rebalances it. Yours is strong and already expressive, so the fix is {helper_el}, the element your Day Master shapes. Translation: less talking, more finishing. You have opinions and energy in abundance. What calms you down is something concrete with a deadline and a result you can point at. Yeon's practical version: when you catch yourself lecturing, ask what you could finish today. Then go finish it.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Your fix element is {helper_el}. Less talking, more finishing.

wood.text: In daily life, {helper_el} means growth and fresh starts. Learn something, plant something, take the long walk. When you're growing, you're too busy to be petty, and growth is a great look on everyone.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Wood fix: learn something new. Hard to be petty while growing.

fire.text: In daily life, {helper_el} means warmth and visibility. Sunlight, laughter, friends who light up when you arrive, saying the thing out loud. People who are warmed rarely need to be defensive.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Fire fix: sunlight and people who are happy to see you.

earth.text: In daily life, {helper_el} means routine and grounding. Regular meals, a bedtime, a tidy-ish home, plans you keep. A boring structure under you makes all your best qualities steadier.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Earth fix: eat, sleep, repeat. Boring works. Annoyingly.

metal.text: In daily life, {helper_el} means edges. Decisions, decluttering, a clear no, finishing what you started. Clearing out what you don't need makes room for what you do.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Metal fix: clear the junk drawer. Then the junk commitments.

water.text: In daily life, {helper_el} means rest and reflection. Sleep, quiet, journaling, a swim, an evening with no plans. Most bad decisions are tired decisions.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Water fix: go to bed. Seriously. Nothing good is decided at 2am.

rat.text: Saju calls the branch under your Day Master the spouse palace, the you that partners meet at home. Yours is the Rat, 子, deep winter Water, one of the four peach-blossom branches. Yeon's read: charming at night, cagey by day. You flirt brilliantly, keep secrets professionally and let people in about as fast as a bank vault opens. Partners feel the charm and then the wall, and they don't know which one is real. Both are. Pick one person and give them the code. Yeon's footnote: yours is a peach-blossom branch, the charm stars. You attract people without trying, which is lovely and also how you end up with a phone full of almost-somethings. Charm opens doors. It doesn't decide which one you walk through. You do.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Rat spouse palace: charming at midnight, vault by morning. Give someone the code.

ox.text: Saju calls the branch under your Day Master the spouse palace, the you that partners meet at home. Yours is the Ox, 丑, cold wet Earth storing Metal. Yeon's read: loyal to the point of stubborn. Once you've decided how home works, it works that way, forever. Your partner suggested moving the couch in 2022 and you're still thinking about it. Steady is lovely. Immovable is a lot. Say yes to one change you'd normally veto. Yeon's footnote: yours is a storehouse branch. You store things: grudges, hopes, receipts, the exact words from that fight. It makes you deep and a little hard to read. Clear the storehouse now and then, out loud, with the person it concerns.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Ox spouse palace: they asked to move the couch two years ago. Just move the couch.

tiger.text: Saju calls the branch under your Day Master the spouse palace, the you that partners meet at home. Yours is the Tiger, 寅, early-spring Wood with Fire inside, a travel branch. Yeon's read: passionate, protective and restless. You love hard and then get twitchy the moment it feels routine. Partners get the best adventures of their lives and the occasional vanishing act. Tell them when the restlessness hits, before you act on it. Yeon's footnote: yours is a travel branch, yeokma, the moving horse. You get restless at home and in love, and you call it needing space. Sometimes it is. Sometimes it's boredom with good PR. Learn the difference before you book the flight.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Tiger spouse palace: great adventures, sudden vanishings. Announce the twitch.

rabbit.text: Saju calls the branch under your Day Master the spouse palace, the you that partners meet at home. Yours is the Rabbit, 卯, pure spring Wood, a peach-blossom branch. Yeon's read: soft, stylish and allergic to conflict. You'll redecorate the whole apartment to avoid one awkward conversation. The home looks beautiful. The conversation is still waiting. Have it before the throw pillows multiply further. Yeon's footnote: yours is a peach-blossom branch, the charm stars. You attract people without trying, which is lovely and also how you end up with a phone full of almost-somethings. Charm opens doors. It doesn't decide which one you walk through. You do.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Rabbit spouse palace: new throw pillows instead of one hard talk. Have the talk.

dragon.text: Saju calls the branch under your Day Master the spouse palace, the you that partners meet at home. Yours is the Dragon, 辰, damp spring Earth, a storehouse branch. Say what you hope for, and let them answer it. Yeon's footnote: yours is a storehouse branch. You store things: grudges, hopes, receipts, the exact words from that fight. It makes you deep and a little hard to read. Clear the storehouse now and then, out loud, with the person it concerns.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Dragon spouse palace: they're failing a test they've never seen. Share the syllabus.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Pig spouse palace: excusing everything isn't kindness. It's a doormat with manners.

sin-metal.first-impression: Sin, strangers think: put together. The outfit, the posture, the very specific coffee order. You notice everything and you're polite about it, mostly. Ten seconds in, people can tell you have taste, and maybe also that you're slightly judging their shoes. You are. We both know you are. What they don't see: you're sensitive. Very. A careless comment can sting for days behind a perfectly composed face, and you'll replay it while doing your skincare, word by word. Maybe tell someone when it happens, out loud, on the day.
sin-metal.your-red-flag: Let's start with the red one: perfectionism with a side of silent judgment. You have standards for everything, and you grade everyone quietly, then feel disappointed when they fail criteria they didn't know existed. You also take small slights personally and keep them polished in a little display case, lit nicely, labeled by date. People think you're cool and above it. Actually, you're hurt and far too elegant to say so. That's a lot of energy spent on looking unbothered when you could just mention it. Saying that stung is extremely chic, actually.
sin-metal.how-you-sabotage-love: Romantically, you want to be treasured, and you should be. But you sometimes test people instead of telling them what you need. Your sabotage is falling for an ideal and then being let down by the real, slightly chaotic human. You also play it cool when you care, waiting hours to reply so you seem unbothered. Unbothered isn't attractive. Honest is. Real people have flaws. So do real jewels, by the way. They're called inclusions, and they're how you tell a real stone from a fake one. Be the real one.
sin-metal.friends-and-work: At work you deliver quality: polished, precise, impeccable. Also slow, because nothing is ever finished, it's just abandoned at 2am when you finally give up on perfect. Criticism hurts far more than you let anyone see. With friends you're thoughtful, the perfect gift giver, the one with the excellent recommendations. But you can be picky about friends to the point of loneliness. Not everyone needs to be fully polished to be worth keeping. Some of the best people are a bit rough around the edges. Let a few of them in.
sin-metal.the-lie: The line you repeat when nobody's listening: I just have high standards. Sometimes it's high standards. Sometimes it's fear of being seen trying and failing in public. You also tell yourself you're fine alone because people are disappointing. Some are, sure. But some would genuinely surprise you if you let them see the unpolished version: the bad day, the messy room, the unfiltered opinion. That version is more lovable than you think. It's certainly more interesting. Show one person the messy draft of you this month. Watch them like you more, not less. It's almost annoying how well it works.
sin-metal.the-fix: Here's the fix, approved by Bom. Finish something at ninety percent and send it anyway. Tell one person something that hurt, right when it happens, in plain words. Do one thing badly on purpose: karaoke, a sketch, dancing at a wedding. In love, say what you need instead of testing whether they'll guess. You're a jewel: rare, sharp, beautiful. You don't need to be flawless to be precious. Nobody does. Not even you. Especially not you. Okay, that was almost sweet. Moving on. Seriously, ninety percent is plenty. Nobody else can see the last ten.

sin-metal.speaker: yeon
sin-metal.text: Sin. You've judged three outfits and a font since we started.

sin-metal.speaker: yeon
sin-metal.text: Great taste. And a secret scorecard nobody agreed to.

sin-metal.speaker: yeon
sin-metal.text: Waiting three hours to reply isn't mystery, Sin. It's homework for them. Unbothered isn't a love language.

sin-metal.speaker: yeon
sin-metal.text: True. Now do karaoke badly. On purpose. Character building.

spring.intro:
Spring-born Sin: Wood ran the season and Metal shapes Wood, so you're a jewel in a shop full of options with opinions about every single one. Stylish, sharp and very particular. People clock your taste in ten seconds. Your red flag is the eternal upgrade. Nothing is ever quite right: the restaurant, the outfit, the partner. You're always browsing. In love you keep one eye on the exit in case something better comes along. At work you redesign the project before finishing it. The fix: pick something, commit and stop comparing for a month. Contentment is a skill, and you've been skipping practice.

Yeon's seasonal note: spring babies start things with enormous enthusiasm and abandon about half of them by June. Before you start the next big thing, finish one small old thing. Just one.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: You returned the same jacket three times. Then you bought it again. Sin.

summer.intro:
Summer Sin, you were born while Fire was in charge and Fire tests Metal, so you were polished under heat and now you flinch at every spark. You're elegant, gracious and secretly devastated by mild feedback. People see someone composed and stylish. Your friends know one comment about your haircut ruined your week. Your red flag is sensitivity disguised as poise. You smile, then replay the comment for days and quietly withdraw. In love you take small criticism as total rejection. At work you go icy when someone edits your work. The fix: when feedback stings, ask whether it's about you or about the thing. It's usually the thing.

Yeon's seasonal note: summer babies run hot. Big feelings, big plans, big crashes. Schedule the crash: one lazy day a week, on purpose, so it doesn't schedule itself at the worst time.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Someone said 'interesting fringe' and you thought about it for nine days, Sin.

autumn.intro:
Autumn Sin, Metal ran your birth month and doubled your element, so you're the jewel in the glass case and you'd like everyone to admire from a distance. Refined, proud, exquisite taste. People find you a bit intimidating. Your friends know you're softer than you look and would never admit it. Your red flag is pride as a security system. You don't apologize easily, you don't ask twice and you never chase. In love partners feel judged. At work your standards are brilliant and also exhausting for everyone near them. The fix: say I was wrong once this month, sincerely, with no clever follow-up line.

Yeon's seasonal note: autumn babies judge. Gently, accurately, constantly. Give one person a pass this week they haven't technically earned. It's good practice.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: You'd rather eat glass than say sorry first. Try it once, Sin. Glass optional.

winter.intro:
Winter Sin, you were born while Water was in charge and Metal generates Water, so your sparkle comes out as wit. Dry, precise, slightly devastating. People see someone clever and a bit aloof. Your friends know your one-liners are how you avoid saying anything real. Your red flag is sarcasm as armor. Someone gets close, you make a joke. Someone compliments you, you deflect with a better joke. In love partners get your best material and none of your actual feelings. At work you're the funniest person in the room and the hardest to read. The fix: next time you feel something, say it straight before you reach for the punchline.

Yeon's seasonal note: winter babies hibernate and call it being busy. People miss you. Go outside, see a friend, reply to the thing.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Sin is so funny! Sin is also allowed to say something sincere.

earth.intro:
Earth days end every season, and you were born in them, Sin: a jewel in rich soil, supported and a little buried. People see someone elegant and composed. Your friends know you're editing everyone, quietly, all the time. Your red flag is silent judgment. In love you notice the flaw and wait to see if they fix it unprompted. At work your standards are high and almost never stated. The fix: say one standard out loud before you hold anyone to it. Unspoken rules aren't fair.

Yeon's seasonal note: Earth-days babies absorb everyone's mood and call it being supportive. Some of it is just sponging. Wring yourself out regularly.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Sin has great taste. Tell people what it is before you grade them!

sin-metal.strong: Strong chart, Sin. Well set, well polished and very aware of it. The blind spot: you're a snob, darling. Lovingly. Your standards are high enough that people feel judged walking into your flat. In love you notice the shoes, the grammar, the restaurant choice, and you mark points off silently. With friends you're the self-appointed arbiter of taste. The fix: compliment something you'd never choose yourself, sincerely. Taste isn't one correct answer, and joy isn't a design award. Let people enjoy their beige sofas.
sin-metal.weak: Weak chart, Sin, so your sparkle depends a lot on outside lighting. Translation: you need reassurance more than you admit. The blind spot: perfectionism as protection. If everything you post, say and wear is flawless, nobody can criticize. Exhausting. In love one careless remark lands like a crack in the stone. At work you over-prepare and still feel like a fraud. The fix: post something unedited. Send a message without rereading it four times. Discover that people like you scratched.

group-chat.text:
You're the curator, Sin. You share the best links, the most beautiful photos, the restaurant everyone ends up loving. Your taste is the group's quiet standard. Honest Yeon note: you judge the chat's choices silently, and it shows. A delayed reply, a single "interesting," an emoji that's technically positive and spiritually not. Your friends can feel you rating the dinner plan. Be generous with one thing this week that isn't up to your standard.

Also, you edit your messages after sending them. Everyone sees "edited." Nobody cares about the typo. They care that you replied. Let one imperfect message stand as it is this week.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Sin, your 'interesting' has a whole review attached. Everyone can hear it.

compliment.text:
You'll take any compliment except one, Sin: that you're enough. People admire your style, your taste, your precision, and you accept it while privately listing what's still wrong. When someone says you're great as you are, you think they haven't looked closely enough. They have. You're allowed to be finished for today. A jewel doesn't need one more polish to be beautiful.

Try a little exercise. Next time you get a compliment, answer only "thank you, that's kind." No correction, no but. Feel how strange it is. Then feel how nice it is.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: You're enough, Sin. Today. As you are.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Stop listing your flaws when someone compliments you. Rude to them, honestly.

ranking.heading: Your toxic traits, ranked
ranking.text: Yeon's ranking of your toxic traits, Sin, from mild to spicy. Third place: being visibly unimpressed by restaurants other people chose. Second place: needing reassurance and refusing to ask for it directly. First place: testing people quietly to see if they'll notice what you want. They fail, you withdraw, nobody knows what happened. The fix: say what you want. Tests are not communication.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Sin's toxic trait number one: secret tests nobody knows they're taking.

seven-days.heading: Your seven-day starter
seven-days.text: Your seven-day starter, Sin. Monday, send a message without editing it. Tuesday, enjoy a restaurant someone else chose. Wednesday, ask directly for something you want. Thursday, wear the thing you've been saving. Friday, accept a compliment with only "thank you." Saturday, spend time near water. Sunday, notice how much energy you saved by not being perfect.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Seven days, Sin. Start with one unedited message.

three-people.heading: What three people would say, if they were brave
three-people.text: What three people would say about you, Sin, if they were brave. Your ex: "Beautiful taste, impossible standards, and I never knew which test I'd failed." Your coworker: "Their work is flawless. They think it isn't." Your best friend: "Picks the perfect gift every time and can't accept a compliment to save their life." All three think you're far more wonderful than you let yourself believe.

work-persona.heading: Your meeting persona
work-persona.text: Your meeting persona, Sin: the slides are beautiful, the critique is precise, and the colleague whose work you critiqued is still recovering. Lead with what's working.
